endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: Training healthcare professionals in recognizing failure modes and offering a simple mechanism to disable autonomous AI when necessary is essential to avoid unchecked errors that could jeopardize patient care.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Product sunset or discontinuation: Defined notice period and required transition support, including export of customer data and any organization-specific configurations in usable form.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Enumerate organizational GAI systems for incorporation into AI system inventory and adjust AI system inventory requirements to account for GAI risks.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether documented, vendor-independent means to disable, halt, or roll back AI shorten the time that a malfunctioning tool affects patients, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on three endorsements, one of which is a multi-society radiology statement written as a requirement.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The three endorsing sources are guidance documents and frameworks. They express expert consensus, and they do not supply effect estimates, comparison groups, or measured outcomes that GRADE could weigh.

The radiology multi-society statement frames a simple disable mechanism as a requirement for autonomous AI. The CHAI playbooks address a related case, vendor sunset, through notice periods and data export. NIST AI 600-1 calls for an inventory of generative AI systems, which a health system would need before it could locate and halt embedded tools.

The radiology statement links training in failure modes with a disable mechanism as a way to keep errors from reaching patients. No supplied study measures how often AI malfunctions persist, how long they persist, or whether a halt procedure intercepts them. The safety benefit therefore remains a stated rationale rather than an observed effect.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that measure time from detection of an AI malfunction to its disablement, with and without documented vendor-independent procedures, and that record patient exposure during that interval. Simulation drills or post-incident reviews could test whether staff can execute rollback procedures as written, and whether compensating controls such as manual workflows or feature toggles work for AI embedded in electronic health records and devices where the health system lacks direct control.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence exists on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have fewer technical staff to maintain and rehearse disable procedures, and whether the practice performs the same way in those settings remains unknown.
